title: The 2018 Konga Sale That Sim Shagaya Says He Did Not Want
dek: Six years after he founded Nigeria's Konga, its investors sold it to Zinox; Shagaya later gave two explanations at once.

story.event: The investors' sale of Konga to Zinox after layoffs and a funding drought, and the founder's later account
story.summary: Sim Shagaya founded the Lagos online retailer Konga in 2012 with $3.5 million from Kinnevik; Kinnevik and Naspers invested heavily as it competed with Jumia. After investors stopped adding money in 2015, Shagaya stepped down as chief executive in January 2016; in late 2017 Konga reportedly cut more than 60 per cent of its staff and ended pay on delivery, and in February 2018 Naspers and Kinnevik sold it to Zinox. Shagaya later said he had not wanted the sale, blamed Nigeria's economy and also his own focus on customer acquisition over margins.
paragraphs: In early February 2018, Zinox, a Nigerian computer maker led by Leo Stan Ekeh, announced that it had taken over Konga, the Lagos online shop that Sim Shagaya had founded six years earlier. The sellers were Konga's big investors, South Africa's Naspers and Sweden's Kinnevik. About two months before, Konga had reportedly laid off more than 60 per cent of its staff and stopped letting customers pay on delivery. Shagaya, who had stepped back from running the company in 2016, later said of the sale: "I'll be honest. I didn't want to do it. It was very painful, very tragic."

He had begun in 2012 with $3.5 million from Kinnevik; a year earlier, Nigeria had only about four million smartphone users. For the first year he paid himself nothing. Jumia, backed by Rocket Internet, launched at almost the same moment, and both companies spent heavily to win customers. Kinnevik and Naspers put in $35 million more by the end of 2013, and Konga grew, by Shagaya's account, about 300 per cent a year.

Then the money around it changed. Oil prices fell from 2014, the economy faltered, and in 2015, Shagaya said, many of Konga's investors decided not to put in more; some stopped investing in Africa altogether. In January 2016, after meeting the investors in Amsterdam, he handed the chief executive's job to his operating chief, Shola Adekoya, and became chairman, telling staff in an email that the change was in the company's interest. His friend Jason Njoku, founder of iROKOtv, wrote at the time of the sale that 95 per cent of Shagaya's material wealth had been tied up in Konga.

Shagaya's account of why it ended has two halves. Konga, he said, started alongside Flipkart in India and Souq in the Middle East, with the same investors, and both were later bought by Walmart and Amazon: "we did everything right but Nigeria did not come to the altar." He also said he had been wrong to treat every customer not won as lost for good, and that "I could have built this very differently," as a smaller, slower business minding its gross margins. At uLesson, which he founded in 2019, he says low-margin opportunities are left to others.

quote.text: If thou have ploughed, gather thine harvest in the field, and the God shall make it great under thine hand.
quote.work: The Instruction of Ptahhotep (and of Ke'gemni)
quote.source_title: The Instruction of Ptah-Hotep and the Instruction of Ke'Gemni, tr. Battiscombe G. Gunn, Project Gutenberg eBook #30508
quote.connection: Ptahhotep's farmer grows by gathering what his own field yields. Shagaya, looking back, half agrees: Konga could have lived on its margins. He also says it did everything right and the country did not come to the altar. The proverb does not settle which account is truer.

reflection: Shagaya does not choose one explanation, and that seems honest. Some of what happens to a company is weather: an oil price, an election, investors changing their minds about a continent. Some of it is choices made inside, like how fast to spend. And the cost of both landed on the people who lost their jobs.

When something of yours goes wrong, it is tempting to pick one story, either the conditions or yourself. The first protects you and the second punishes you; neither teaches much alone. Keeping both in view, plainly, is how the next thing gets built more carefully.
invitation: Think of one recent disappointment in your work. Write one sentence on what was outside your control and one on what you would do differently, then leave both there for today.

cross_checks.claim: Shagaya founded Konga in 2012 with $3.5 million from Kinnevik.
In January 2016, after meeting investors in Amsterdam, Shagaya stepped down as CEO and became chairman, with Shola Adekoya taking over.
In February 2018 Zinox acquired Konga from Naspers and Kinnevik.
Shortly before the sale Konga laid off a large share of its staff and ended pay on delivery.
Konga competed from the start with Rocket Internet-backed Jumia.

research_notes: The slate framed this as Shagaya 'selling' Konga, but the sellers were the majority investors, Naspers and Kinnevik (Vanguard, ThisDay); Shagaya had stepped down as CEO in January 2016 and says he did not want the sale, so the story presents it as the investors' sale and his account of it, and arc is 'setback' rather than 'change-of-direction'. Blame is given only as Shagaya himself puts it (both the Nigerian economy and his own focus on customer acquisition); Jason Njoku's view that there was overspending is not used. Layoffs: Techpoint (December 2017) said Konga 'reportedly' laid off over 60 per cent of its workforce; Wikipedia says 'over half'; ThisDay mentions staff 'laid off in the restructuring process' without a figure; no headcount is given. Price: no price was confirmed in the cited reports; a $10 million figure circulates (attributed to ThisDay in search results and called a rumour elsewhere) and Vanguard says Konga was 'said to worth $34 million'; neither is used. Negotiation length: Vanguard says a month-long negotiation, ThisDay 'months of strategic negotiations'; the story gives no length. Funding: TechCabal (2014) gives $3.5 million seed (2012), $10 million Series A (2013) and $25 million Series B (December 2013); later rounds (a reported 2014 Series C) are not used. The 300 per cent growth figure is Shagaya's own claim and is attributed. Njoku's 95 per cent figure is his statement in a Medium post, quoted by BellaNaija (medium.com is 403). The no-salary detail comes from Shagaya's own words in an earlier Pulse/My Africa Podcast interview (single source, his own account). The Techpoint profile and two older Techpoint reports are cited from Internet Archive copies because techpoint.africa returns 403. The Ptahhotep maxim is applied by analogy.
